subject: Mathematics
title: Fundamental Laws of Trigonometry
learningOutcomes: Establish the fundamental law \(\cos(\alpha-\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\beta\) from the distance formula and the unit circle.
Derive \(\cos(\alpha+\beta)\), \(\sin(\alpha\pm\beta)\) and \(\tan(\alpha\pm\beta)\) from the fundamental law and use them to find exact values.
Find the ratios of the allied angles \(\frac{\pi}{2}\pm\theta\), \(\pi\pm\theta\), \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\pm\theta\) and \(2\pi\pm\theta\).
Express \(a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta\) in the form \(r\sin(\theta+\varphi)\) and find its maximum and minimum values.
Derive and use the double angle identities for \(\sin2\alpha\), \(\cos2\alpha\) and \(\tan2\alpha\).
Derive and use the half angle identities, choosing the correct sign from the quadrant of \(\frac{\theta}{2}\).
Derive and use the triple angle identities for \(\sin3\alpha\), \(\cos3\alpha\) and \(\tan3\alpha\).
Express a product of sines and cosines as a sum or difference.
Express a sum or difference of sines and cosines as a product.

sections.heading: The Fundamental Law
sections.body: Place the points \(A(1,0)\), \(B(\cos(\alpha-\beta),\sin(\alpha-\beta))\), \(C(\cos\beta,\sin\beta)\) and \(D(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)\) on the unit circle. Chords \(AB\) and \(CD\) subtend the same angle \(\alpha-\beta\) at the centre, so \(AB=CD\). Writing \(AB^2=CD^2\) with the distance formula gives \(\cos(\alpha-\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\beta\). Every other formula of the unit comes from this one.

sections.heading: Sum and Difference Formulas
sections.body: Replacing \(\beta\) by \(-\beta\) gives \(\cos(\alpha+\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta\). Using \(\sin\theta=\cos(90^\circ-\theta)\) gives \(\sin(\alpha\pm\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta\pm\cos\alpha\sin\beta\), and dividing sine by cosine gives \(\tan(\alpha\pm\beta)=\dfrac{\tan\alpha\pm\tan\beta}{1\mp\tan\alpha\tan\beta}\). The formulas give exact values such as \(\cos15^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\).

sections.heading: Allied Angles
sections.body: Allied angles are \(\frac{\pi}{2}\pm\theta\), \(\pi\pm\theta\), \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\pm\theta\) and \(2\pi\pm\theta\). Ask two questions. Is the angle an odd multiple of \(90^\circ\)? Then sine and cosine (tangent and cotangent) swap. Which quadrant is it in, taking \(\theta\) as acute? That quadrant (ASTC) gives the sign. For example \(\sin(90^\circ+\theta)=\cos\theta\) and \(\cos(180^\circ-\theta)=-\cos\theta\).

sections.heading: The Form r sin(θ + φ)
sections.body: For \(a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta\) put \(a=r\cos\varphi\) and \(b=r\sin\varphi\). Then \(a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta=r\sin(\theta+\varphi)\) with \(r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\), \(\cos\varphi=\frac{a}{r}\) and \(\sin\varphi=\frac{b}{r}\). The maximum value is \(r\) and the minimum is \(-r\). Choose \(\varphi\) from the signs of \(\cos\varphi\) and \(\sin\varphi\), not from \(\tan^{-1}\frac{b}{a}\) alone.

sections.heading: Double Angle Identities
sections.body: Put \(\beta=\alpha\) in the sum formulas: \(\sin2\alpha=2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha\), \(\cos2\alpha=\cos^2\alpha-\sin^2\alpha=2\cos^2\alpha-1=1-2\sin^2\alpha\) and \(\tan2\alpha=\dfrac{2\tan\alpha}{1-\tan^2\alpha}\). Rearranged, they give the power-reduction identities \(\cos^2\alpha=\frac{1+\cos2\alpha}{2}\) and \(\sin^2\alpha=\frac{1-\cos2\alpha}{2}\).

sections.heading: Half Angle Identities
sections.body: Replacing \(\alpha\) by \(\frac{\theta}{2}\) gives \(\sin\frac{\theta}{2}=\pm\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos\theta}{2}}\), \(\cos\frac{\theta}{2}=\pm\sqrt{\frac{1+\cos\theta}{2}}\) and \(\tan\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1-\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=\frac{\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta}\). The sign of the root is taken from the quadrant of \(\frac{\theta}{2}\), not of \(\theta\).

sections.heading: Triple Angle Identities
sections.body: Write \(3\alpha=2\alpha+\alpha\): \(\sin3\alpha=3\sin\alpha-4\sin^3\alpha\), \(\cos3\alpha=4\cos^3\alpha-3\cos\alpha\) and \(\tan3\alpha=\dfrac{3\tan\alpha-\tan^3\alpha}{1-3\tan^2\alpha}\). A quick check is \(\alpha=30^\circ\): \(\sin90^\circ=3\cdot\frac12-4\cdot\frac18=1\).

sections.heading: Product to Sum and Sum to Product
sections.body: Adding and subtracting the sum and difference formulas gives \(2\sin\alpha\cos\beta=\sin(\alpha+\beta)+\sin(\alpha-\beta)\), \(2\cos\alpha\sin\beta=\sin(\alpha+\beta)-\sin(\alpha-\beta)\), \(2\cos\alpha\cos\beta=\cos(\alpha+\beta)+\cos(\alpha-\beta)\) and \(2\sin\alpha\sin\beta=\cos(\alpha-\beta)-\cos(\alpha+\beta)\). Put \(\alpha=\frac{p+q}{2}\), \(\beta=\frac{p-q}{2}\) to read them backwards, for example \(\sin p+\sin q=2\sin\frac{p+q}{2}\cos\frac{p-q}{2}\).

definitions.definition: An equation that is true for every angle for which both sides are defined, such as \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\).
\(\cos(\alpha-\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\beta\), from which all other identities of the unit are derived.
Angles of the form \(\frac{\pi}{2}\pm\theta\), \(\pi\pm\theta\), \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\pm\theta\), \(2\pi\pm\theta\), whose ratios reduce to ratios of \(\theta\).
The sign rule for the quadrants: All positive in I, Sine in II, Tangent in III, Cosine in IV.
Sine and cosine, tangent and cotangent, secant and cosecant swap when an odd multiple of \(90^\circ\) is involved.
In \(a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta=r\sin(\theta+\varphi)\), the number \(r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\), the largest value of the expression.
The angle \(2\alpha\), whose ratios are \(\sin2\alpha=2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha\), \(\cos2\alpha=\cos^2\alpha-\sin^2\alpha\) and \(\tan2\alpha=\frac{2\tan\alpha}{1-\tan^2\alpha}\).
The angle \(\frac{\theta}{2}\); \(\sin\frac{\theta}{2}=\pm\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos\theta}{2}}\) with the sign from its own quadrant.
Rewriting \(\sin^2\alpha\) and \(\cos^2\alpha\) with \(\cos2\alpha\) so that no square is left.
A formula that turns \(2\sin\alpha\cos\beta\) (or a similar product) into a sum or difference of single ratios.
A formula that turns \(\sin p\pm\sin q\) or \(\cos p\pm\cos q\) into a product, using \(\frac{p+q}{2}\) and \(\frac{p-q}{2}\).

examTips: The board paper nearly always asks you to prove \(\cos(\alpha-\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta+\sin\alpha\sin\beta\): learn the figure with the four points \(A,B,C,D\) and the equal chords \(AB=CD\).
Cosine of a sum has a minus sign, \(\cos(\alpha+\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta\). Sine keeps the sign: \(\sin(\alpha\pm\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta\pm\cos\alpha\sin\beta\).
For allied angles ask two questions: does the name change (odd multiple of \(90^\circ\))? and which quadrant, so which sign (ASTC, with \(\theta\) acute)?
Learn \(\sin15^\circ=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}\), \(\cos15^\circ=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}\) and \(\tan15^\circ=2-\sqrt3\); write the exact value, not a decimal.
In \(a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta=r\sin(\theta+\varphi)\) choose \(\varphi\) from the signs of \(\cos\varphi\) and \(\sin\varphi\). If \(a<0\), \(\tan^{-1}\frac{b}{a}\) alone gives the wrong quadrant.
Pick the form of \(\cos2\alpha\) that matches what you know: \(1-2\sin^2\alpha\) with \(\sin\alpha\), \(2\cos^2\alpha-1\) with \(\cos\alpha\).
For half angles take the sign from the quadrant of \(\frac{\theta}{2}\), not of \(\theta\). \(\tan\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1-\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\) needs no \(\pm\).
Before using a product-to-sum formula make the coefficient \(2\); \(\sin\alpha\sin\beta\) always gives (difference) minus (sum). Only \(\cos p-\cos q\) has the factor \(-2\).
Test any doubtful formula at \(30^\circ\) or \(45^\circ\): a true identity holds for every angle, so one failure proves it wrong.
